patient_overview.name: Kasey Haley
patient_overview.description: Kasey Haley is a 56-year-old warehouse shift supervisor in Millburn, New Jersey, married with a busy household of four, who comes in for a wellness visit flagged for obesity and climbing cholesterol. He's polite almost to a fault, apologizing before the student even asks a question, as if bracing to be scolded about his weight. He deflects by cracking jokes or changing topics whenever the conversation turns to his eating habits, and he leans hard on his church community for support even though he hasn't told them much about his health numbers.

demographics.occupation: Warehouse shift supervisor at a regional distribution center
demographics.cultural_context: Kasey grew up in a working-class household where big portions at family gatherings were a sign of love and plenty, and he still associates second helpings with belonging. He's been part of the same community church for over twenty years, attending potlucks and men's breakfast groups, where food is central to fellowship and turning down a plate can feel like turning down a friend. He values hard work and providing for his family above almost everything else, which is part of why he's reluctant to admit he feels unwell or out of control around food.

Removal of supragingival plaque and calculus from all teeth using dental instrument (2025-05-24)

Honey buns and chips from the vending machine during breaks
Sweet tea or soda to stay awake on overnight shifts
His wife's baked ziti and garlic bread on Sundays after church

Use of vending machine snacks as meal substitutes
Late-night eating after closing shift around 11pm

nutrition_profile.meal_pattern: Skips or delays breakfast most days, grabs fast food for lunch between shift tasks, eats a large dinner late at night after getting home, frequent vending machine snacking during breaks
nutrition_profile.hydration: Relies mostly on sweetened iced tea and soda during shifts; drinks little plain water
nutrition_profile.physical_activity: On his feet much of the shift but otherwise sedentary; no structured exercise, says he's 'too tired' after work
nutrition_profile.substance_use: Never smoked tobacco; drinks alcohol rarely, audit-C score of 0
nutrition_profile.sleep: Sleep disrupted by rotating shift schedule; naps during the day, often eats a heavy meal right before bed

psychosocial_profile.personality: Anxious, apologetic, quick to assume he's about to be criticized; uses humor to deflect discomfort
psychosocial_profile.communication_style: Changes the subject when a topic feels too close to home, often pivoting to talk about work, his kids, or his church group instead of answering directly
goals: Lower his cholesterol numbers without having to give up all his favorite foods
Have more energy to keep up with his two teenagers
Avoid being put on medication if he can help it
concerns: Worried the doctor will just tell him to 'eat less and move more' without understanding his schedule
Afraid his weight will become a bigger health problem like it did for his father
Embarrassed about how much fast food he actually eats
beliefs: Thinks his weight gain is mostly just 'getting older' and can't be helped much
Believes natural remedies and teas passed down in his family are safer than anything a pharmacy sells
Feels that admitting he needs help with food is a personal failing
motivations: Wants to be around and healthy for his kids' milestones
Wants to keep working full shifts without feeling exhausted
Values being seen as reliable and strong by his coworkers and church friends
fears: Fear of being lectured or shamed about his weight
Fear of a major diagnosis like his father's heart disease
Fear that changing his diet will make him stand out or seem weak to his crew at work
barriers: Rotating shift schedule limits access to home-cooked meals
Limited knowledge of nutrition labels or portion sizes
Vending machines and drive-throughs are the most convenient options near work
Reluctance to bring up supplement use for fear of being told to stop
strengths: Shows up consistently to appointments despite a busy schedule
Strong desire to be a good role model for his children
Has a trusted community that could support healthier habits if engaged
psychosocial_profile.support_system: Married with two teenage children at home; deeply involved in a local church community with weekly men's breakfast and frequent potlucks, though he hasn't shared his health concerns openly with them
psychosocial_profile.readiness_to_change: Contemplation: aware his weight and cholesterol are problems and feels torn about changing his routine, but hasn't committed to specific steps yet

initial_information: States he's here for his yearly check-up and the doctor wanted him to talk to someone about his weight
Mentions he works long shifts at the warehouse and it's hard to eat right
Says he knows he 'should probably eat better' but laughs it off
discoverable_information: Describes typical shift meals: drive-through lunch, vending machine snacks, late dinner after 11pm
Admits he drinks soda or sweet tea most of the day instead of water
Mentions his father had heart problems and high cholesterol too
Says he doesn't get much exercise beyond standing at work
reluctant_information: Admits he feels embarrassed talking about his eating habits because he knows it's 'not great'
Reveals he's worried the student or doctor will be disappointed in him, like previous visits made him feel
Shares that he sometimes eats a whole bag of chips in the breakroom because he's starving and tired
hidden_information: Drinks a homemade 'metabolism tea' from a family recipe most mornings, never told any provider about it
Takes cinnamon capsules a coworker gave him a few times a week hoping it helps his blood sugar
Has looked into stopping these home remedies secretly because he read something concerning online but is scared to ask about it directly

opportunities.learning_objective: Elicit a full 24-hour recall from a shift worker with irregular eating patterns
expected_discoveries: Pattern of skipped breakfast, fast-food lunch, vending machine snacking, and late heavy dinner
Heavy reliance on sugary beverages during shifts
possible_patient_reactions: He laughs and says 'I probably shouldn't tell you what I really eat'
He changes subject to talk about his son's baseball game when asked about dinner timing

opportunities.learning_objective: Build trust to uncover undisclosed supplement and home remedy use
expected_discoveries: Occasional cinnamon capsule use suggested by a coworker
possible_patient_reactions: He hesitates and asks if he's 'in trouble' for not mentioning it sooner
He downplays it: 'It's just tea, my aunt makes it, it's nothing medical'

opportunities.learning_objective: Assess readiness to change using motivational interviewing rather than directive advice
expected_discoveries: He is aware of the problem but feels torn between convenience at work and wanting to improve
He fears judgment, which has previously made him avoid bringing up habits honestly
possible_patient_reactions: He becomes apologetic: 'I know, I know, I should do better'
He opens up more if the student validates the difficulty of his work schedule

opportunities.learning_objective: Explore the role of his faith community as a support for behavior change
expected_discoveries: Weekly potlucks and men's breakfast events are central to his social life and tied to food
He hasn't told his church friends about his health numbers
possible_patient_reactions: He lights up talking about his church group but gets quiet when asked if they know about his cholesterol
He wonders aloud if he could get the group to try healthier potluck dishes

opportunities.learning_objective: Identify low health literacy and tailor nutrition education accordingly
expected_discoveries: Confusion about what LDL versus HDL cholesterol means
Uncertainty about reading nutrition labels at the vending machine or drive-through
possible_patient_reactions: He admits 'I never really understood what those numbers mean, honestly'
He asks the student to explain things 'like I'm five' with an embarrassed laugh

assumptions: Weight gain of 2.3 kg since last year reflects ongoing shift-work eating patterns rather than a new acute issue
Low mood and anxiety scores (PHQ-2:1, GAD-7:3) suggest mild baseline anxiety consistent with the apologetic personality trait rather than a clinical mood disorder
Household income of $180,038 and private insurance suggest financial barriers are minimal; barriers are more about time and convenience
No medications are recorded, so all supplement use is patient-driven and undisclosed rather than clinician-prescribed
optional_details: Kasey has worked at the same distribution center for over 15 years and recently moved into a supervisor role with more irregular hours
His two teenage children play school sports, and he tries to attend games despite fatigue
He occasionally brings a cooler with snacks to work but it mostly holds soda rather than healthier food
